claims.text: Local compositional fluctuations in an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy coating impede dislocation motion during continuous loading.
Short-range ordering in the matrix impedes dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion caused by local compositional fluctuations and short-range ordering enhances creep resistance.
The relevant starting material is a protective coating with an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy microstructure.
Such a coating can be prepared by arc melting or HVOF spraying with a microstructure typical of commercially viable wear- and creep-resistant coatings.
A minor dopant can promote short-range ordering and compositional clustering in the coating.
Temperatures of 500–600 °C or higher are creep-relevant conditions for this coating under constant stress.
Short-range-ordered clusters locally modulate stacking-fault energy.
Short-range-ordered clusters increase local Peierls friction.
Chemical and structural inhomogeneities generated by dopant-induced ordering act as repeated strong pinning points for dislocations.
These pinning sites elevate the local barrier for dislocation glide or climb.
Elevating the barrier to glide or climb reduces the steady-state creep rate.
The doped coating will have a 20–30% lower steady-state creep strain rate than the undoped coating at the same load and temperature.
The doped coating will show increased dislocation tangling and pinned dislocation segments associated with compositional fluctuations.
The undoped baseline has a nominally random elemental distribution and a higher steady-state creep rate.
The ordering-mediated benefit is most pronounced below approximately 700–800 °C because short-range ordering remains stable there.
Dislocation-mediated creep dominates in the proposed lower-temperature operating regime.
At higher temperatures, grain-boundary sliding or diffusion may reduce the contribution of local ordering to creep resistance.
